utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Again today we'll be sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis with Judge Robinson -- I'm sorry, Judge Morrison being away due to his official functions. Good morning, Ms. Edgerton. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Lieutenant-Colonel.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd just like to go back to a couple of things you discussed yesterday and one of them is at page 45 - I'm sorry I don't have the updated page references available - where you discussed the potential for mobilisation of Muslim forces within Sarajevo, and you said that after the war they had 120.000 armed combat amounts in the city. Now, you don't mean to assert that that figure of 120.000 is accurate, do you?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is their information, from their sources. Of course I did not have any other possibilities to check this.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, your own deputy commander, Colonel Sladoje has actually given a statement to Dr. Karadzic's Defence counsel in this case and he says that through the intelligence service he learned that there were 42.000 fighters in the ABiH 1st Corps and their 24-hour mobilisation potential was 71.000 - and that's found in 1D05656, paragraph 1. So that's actually 50.000 less than the figure that you've given and, by Colonel Sladoje's account, that actually comes from your services, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that they mentioned this information when their former commanders wrote about that. It was published in the newspapers and obviously they had an enormous potential.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And whatever potential they might have had, Lieutenant-Colonel, you knew, didn't you, that the morale among the 1st Corps forces was low and continued to diminish as the war went on, their forces were dying in large numbers, they had problems with -- and they had problems with mass desertions; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Such information was available, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, also in your testimony yesterday you spoke on a couple of occasions about laser-guided missiles, talking about shelling, you said that it would have to be laser guided so that an artillery shell would fall somewhere into the street or onto a square. And that wasn't possible given the equipment that existed there. And then at page 65 of yesterday's transcript, again you said: "People on the ground were convinced at first that it was certainly not Serbian forces who had done that, and in my view it was open logic because this took place in a small space, small tight areas. For a mortar or a shell to reach such position, it would have to be laser guided to hit such a spot." And I only want to ask you about this reference to laser guiding missiles or ordnances. The point you were making yesterday, I take it, depends on the assumption that if someone is targeting a small area, a tight place or a narrow street, as you said, so the point that you're making depends on that as opposed to someone just shelling -- generally shelling or randomly shelling a populated area, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During my service, inter alia, I had mortars in my unit while I was a platoon commander, of course, before the war and so on. I know that it was necessary to use at least three missiles to reach close to a specific point and to be able then to shell the area. That was, of course, before the war and so on and so forth. So to have just one shell falling in a specific small area, that's absolutely impossible. I was talking about that, that it could have been brought by a bird or it could have been laser guided, and it couldn't have been otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So if you're aiming at a particular spot as opposed to firing randomly and you don't have a laser guidance system, how far off are you going to be?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This kind of artillery weapon such as cannons, howitzers, mortars, generally speaking, I'm not aware that they can be laser guided. The only ones that can be guided by laser are rocket systems and rocket weapons. So simply, any possibility of using mortar shells with a laser guidance system is not possible. There's no need for me to explain the other thing because a mortar missile or shell simply cannot be laser guided. And for one shell to fall in one specific place, that's impossible. If we had had such abilities, we would have selected more profitable targets probably. We would have selected ammunition depots or a unit that was well prepared and at a position or we would have selected their staff and so on. Why would the Serbs target a market? Poor people -- each and every Serb knew that if there was to be a mistake, that we could cause a reaction of the international public, both international and domestic public. So why would we shell people who were queuing for bread or queuing for water? It was just a motive that the Muslims had to cause revolt of their own citizens against the Serbs, on the one hand, and, on the other hand, to provoke a reaction of the international community.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So let's go back to my question. How far off are you going to be?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only tell you from my own experience, from the time when I was a platoon commander and while I had those mortars under me, it could happen that the first shell was fired and it would fall on one spot. The next one would fall at least 50 metres from the first one. If it was 50 metres, that was good, it could be a hundred metres because the charges were different, the weight of the propellants and the charges was different and the weight of the shells themselves was different. So you could never very precisely determine where it would be, otherwise you wouldn't need any corrections. Corrections are made precisely so that you could hit one specific spot, and in order to fire as a group, you have to correct the aberration. There's always the aberration and when it's 25 metres that you manage to achieve then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Sarenac, do you remember what the question was? Could you ask the question again, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I can, although I think he's -- the Lieutenant-Colonel has made his way around to an answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My question was: So if you're aiming at a particular spot as opposed to firing randomly and you don't have a laser guidance system, how far off are you going to be?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said a while ago only that I tried to explain in more detail, 50 to 100 metre, at least a 50-metre aberration in my experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now -- just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So then, taking into account everything that you've just said, it sounds like, if you're aiming at a particular target, it's going to take at least three shells to engage it, to neutralise it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you could say so. I would accept that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Yesterday Dr. Karadzic showed you a document and that was D3092, and perhaps we could call that up on the screen so that you can be reminded of what Dr. Karadzic showed you. It was an official note regarding an interview with a Mr. Kostic, and when Dr. Karadzic showed you that document he said to you: "I will ask you to show us in this example how you worked and how you obtained intelligence." Now, looking at this document again, you would agree with me that in order for this raw data to become intelligence it needs to be corroborated by other means, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. You can see down here below the title it says: Reference, official note of 27 February 1995. So this was the second interview, the clarification of the issue with regard to this source. However, we did not have the first and only information. He did not provide us with the first information nor did it end with this. Rather, as I already said, this information was forwarded to the security and intelligence organ in the corps and then the corps' intelligence and security organ had at its disposal the intelligence and reconnaissance units, also electronic interception units, wire-tapping, and so on. On the other hand, observers from our own unit, in a group of ten soldiers in every platoon and company there was one soldier who was in charge of observation. He had to observe the air-space, the battle-field, and so on. And only when the conversations and interviews were confirmed -- and to have the information confirmed, this was 1995. We already had an enormous amount of data so we made a selection, what is true and what is not. Immediately here we would do the analysis, and in the corps they would do it when everything was sent to them. No action could be carried out on the basis of our information from the brigade. Something could be initiated only from the corps once they completed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And not everything was sent to the corps, was it?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything was sent to the corps. If something was not sent to them, then it means that that piece of information was not relevant and that on the basis of it you couldn't -- otherwise, what would be the purpose of collecting and writing down information unless the information was sent to the corps, to the higher command, so that the higher command and unit would see if there are any elements for something to be done. So everything was forwarded to the corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now -- so looking at this raw data --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I wonder if we can make the English page a little bit smaller so that the rest of us can have somewhere close to the same amount of text that we see on the B/C/S page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So this raw data doesn't disclose anything about how Mr. Kostic came to learn the information he's providing, does it? This document doesn't disclose that at all?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I will indicate once again the information within brackets: Reference, official note of 27 February 1995 on the interview conducted with Jovan Kostic. In this report all the information is explained, how he came by that, where he had been, and so on. And this is just a continuation of the first note. So in the first note, all of this is explained, and that is to say, there was another note preceding this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And where would we find indications about reliability of the source? Because there's nothing in this note .

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course this note doesn't say that. This note includes specific details that he mentioned in another interview, in the second interview, not in the first one. And as this was sent to the corps for analysis and processing, then we did not provide here. That was provided separately in a report. If a report was written, then it was included in a report, but in this case, this was sent to the corps and it was only there that they made the comparisons. Their analytical department then established everything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have any more questions about this document. I'd like to go on to one other area you discussed yesterday. You -- at page 68 of yesterday's transcript, you gave Dr. Karadzic an account about a sniping of an UNPROFOR French soldier who was killed in a observation post located at the Jewish cemetery. And you talked about being assigned to tour your positions with UNPROFOR. And I'd like to ask you about that. So your evidence is that you personally accompanied UNPROFOR officials to the incident location?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So who did you go with?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, I did not draw up a note about who I went there with, but after that, the television of Republika Srpska wanted to conduct an interview. I'm not sure whether they interviewed them. I resisted for a while because as a high-ranking officer, a major at the time, without the approval of the superior command I had no right to appear on TV. However, from the command of the corps this was approved and they told me that I could give an interview about the findings and so on. And this interview can be found somewhere in the archives of the radio and television of Republika Srpska because I know --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel --

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that it was broadcast on several occasions --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- that's okay, but my question was who you went with, and I take from your answer you didn't -- you don't recall --

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. But I know that I went there with UNPROFOR officers who had come to lodge a protest with the corps command, and then the corps command assigned me as the soldiers from my brigade were there at the line. So they sent me to tour the lines together with them and to assess whether it had been possible for a sniper to fire from our positions --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that is to say, the positions of the Sarajevo-Romanija Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now, this was an incident -- or during this incident, the French soldier was killed at the OP that was on the transit road, wasn't he, at the south end of the Jewish cemetery; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in the south end.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that observation post, that OP, was located almost at the confrontation line; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that area generally, yes, that was built-up area. There were buildings and high-rises and our lines were close, one next to the other, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that incident actually took place in August 1994, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that it was summer in 1994 and now you remind me that it was in August, so probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And yesterday you talked about SRK positions being down the hill from the incident location, but actually having toured the line, as you just said you did, you can confirm to us that SRK positions weren't only down the hill from the observation post but they ran the -- along the whole length of the Jewish cemetery and the whole west -- the whole area to the western side of the Jewish cemetery; correct?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is so. But the position of the Jewish cemetery and the geographical feature in general is such that it was above us. The Muslim positions were located so that they were above us. They were looking at us from above, in that section, all the way to Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, did you know that there was a UN investigation made of this incident? The French military police with the UN forces conducted an investigation?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was how I understood them. As soon as they arrived to the corps command and when I went to make this tour together with them, to visit the locations, the finding that they sent to the corps command is something I'm not aware of, but I know that it was then concluded to the effect that the Serbian side was not to blame.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, actually, I'd like to show you the report, a couple of pages from the report that was made on the investigation, and that report is 65 ter number 24727. And the report's dated the 19th of August. And just before I ask the question I just want to note, can you read English, Lieutenant-Colonel, because, unfortunately, I don't think I have a copy of this in your language and I can read you the relevant passage if you can't.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately not, no. I can't read English.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. This is -- this is a copy of, as I said, the military police company's report on their investigation of this incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I'd like to actually go all the way over to page 7 of this incident -- of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: At the last bullet point at the bottom of this page above item number 2, we see the last of a series of conclusions that the military police arrived at following their investigation. They wrote: "It is impossible to determine exactly which side is responsible for this murder because no other UN soldier can explain the exact position of the blue helmet ... before he was killed." So UNPROFOR seems to have come to a different conclusion than you've indicated with respect to the cause of death of the soldier, haven't they?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, obviously, and they said this knowing the activities of our soldiers and knowing that at Zlatiste, above the Jewish cemetery, some Muslim forces were deployed. They were part of the 15th Mountain Brigade. So we actually knew and it was clear to us that fire had not come from our side. In addition to their findings, we were certain that the fire had not come from our side.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's go over to page 9 of this document, and at page 9 you'll see --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And perhaps we could blow it up for the Lieutenant-Colonel just so he can see it as clearly as possible. I think we could make the whole -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: At page 9 you see the confrontation lines between your forces and the Bosnian forces mapped out, the area in question, that's the black line. And then you see a small wedge above the white text box in the corner. The bottom line of the wedge is marked with a number 1 and that's the observation line or indicated as being the observation line of the killed soldier. The point of the wedge, that's item number -- marked as number 3 is the observation post on the transit road, as you know. And the line above the top line of the wedge is marked with item number 2 is the line of fire of the shooting, which, Lieutenant-Colonel, covers a substantial area within Serb-held territory in Grbavica and actually is completely and far away from the potential line of fire you've just indicated at Zlatiste, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a small map, of course, and Zlatiste is this whole geographic feature up there, right above the transit line. In other words, the Jewish cemetery is part of Zlatiste, in fact, but is just called differently. I can see this but I can't give you any other opinion or explanation than I've already done.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, it appears, actually, that the information you gave as to the potential source of fire or line of fire is inaccurate based on the military police investigations, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course I did not have this -- these findings of theirs available. When I was part of their team, they did not conduct an on-site investigation. So I couldn't point out to them on the ground right then and there because they didn't know every feature and every point and so on, so I couldn't point out to them that there were other positions above. However, at that point in time, this position where the observation post was was not physically visible from our side.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your evidence is that this observation post was not physically visible anywhere from the whole expanse of Serb-held territory indicated to its west on this map, the observation post which would have been placed at that location so as to be able to observe the front lines, Lieutenant-Colonel?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That is my conclusion, or rather, we found that out. We knew that it wasn't visible; however, from our positions, because they were on a higher position in relation to us, they could observe our activities and our positions without us being able to see them. There are also buildings below there and certain vegetation and so on so that he could and was in a position to be able to observe us without us being able to see him because of where he was, of his position.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll have nothing further, but I wonder if we could have this page of this document marked as a Prosecution exhibit, given the extensive discussion on it, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What page do you refer to?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This is page 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Only page 9?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think it would also be good -- we don't have any objection to that. I think it would also be good to put in page 7 which was referred to earlier which contains the conclusions of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And as well as the first page. Yes, we'll admit three pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6187, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any re-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. I have a few. But I would like to make an intervention in the transcript, page 13, on lines 5 and 6, the Lieutenant-Colonel said, "They were not visible from our positions." And the Lieutenant-Colonel keeps talking about "positions," the positions of the VRS. Now, could we please have the image that the document we've just seen before, could we see it on the screens, page 7 first and then on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lieutenant-Colonel, sir, I will read the first paragraph for you in English slowly and that will be interpreted to you. [In English] "The soldier Carbonnel was hit by one bullet only in the course of the cross-fire between the opposing parties ..." [Interpretation] Cross-fire. So was this execution or was this in the course -- in cross-fire in fact?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question meant for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, Lieutenant-Colonel. It is their claim here that he was killed in cross-fire between the two sides. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first version when they first talked about this, there was no mention of that possibility. There was only talk about him being killed by a sniper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, that's page 9 or the third page of the adopted -- the admitted document. You talked about positions, dominant positions, and inferior positions in geographic terms. On this map, can we see who was on a higher position and who was at the lower position?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, you can't see that because this is not a topographic map -- I mean, it is but this part which shows the settled area, the built-up area, you cannot really see that. You can only see it if you're on the ground. Because below the transit road, that is a depression, a slope. It -- this part here slopes down towards Grbavica from the transit road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But in terms of the Jewish cemetery, please look at the western-most and the eastern-most border. Which area is lower and which one is dominant in this map, can you tell?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the western border is lower than the eastern in comparison to the Jewish cemetery, so the one towards the transit is lower.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And who was on these -- on this elevation towards Debelo Brdo? Who controlled that part? It's all the way to the south of this map --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, we could just look at the map that the Lieutenant-Colonel marked yesterday as to who controlled Debelo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see a problem asking the witness here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Debelo Brdo, if I can find my bearings here, was under Muslim control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you were asked about the accuracy of the lines. Now, in your interviews, did you check what this defector, this person who had crossed over, knew about the lines or what he knew about the firing positions?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, the accurate positions were determined by certain features that were used as reference points showing that there was something at that place. There was -- there were -- there was military personnel in the features. The weapons were outside in the field. Now, in this particular case that's how it was. Now, we were not able to get from him specific geographic co-ordinates, but he was able to just tell us about certain features that -- and that's how we could determine where that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do -- if you have your statement before you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would appreciate the Trial Chamber allowing the statement to use his statement, if we could perhaps pull it up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I don't have it before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I can read out a portion of it, although it hasn't been admitted, but just as a reminder. You were asked how you established what --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What -- yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't think it's appropriate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- to put his statement to him, his draft statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I don't -- Mr. Karadzic didn't indicate why his showing this document is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I can indicate that because I was the one who suggested Dr. Karadzic do this. The point is, in his statement he has identified certain documents as showing the locations of places where there were military objects, legitimate military objects in Sarajevo. And it's our intention to make a bar table motion at the end of his testimony to admit those documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why could he not have done during his direct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because that would take about four to six hours, so that was the whole purpose of making the map because you wouldn't admit the documents as associated exhibits so we came to the quandary of how to not use our 300 hours unnecessarily. So we had the map drawn and which depicts the military objects that are identified in these documents. But yesterday, Ms. Edgerton pointed out that there was some variation in the map, for example, with the dentistry ministry, between where he marked it and where the location was. So we think that the documents will help you determine exactly what those military objects were. So what we would like to do is now simply ask the witness by showing his statement about how he came to draw this map and to establish that the map was based upon these documents which are reliable and which are based on information received by him or his service. Once we've done that, we can then make a bar table motion and there will be no question as to the provenance of those documents we're seeking to admit through the bar table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That being the case, still why does he need to rely on his draft statement? Can he not lead it directly without relying on the document -- statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, the statement contains references to the numbers of the documents, so by showing him the statement and having him confirm that -- there's three paragraphs in the statement that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So why don't we use a map and without relying on the document put the question to the witness without the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, if we do that, then there won't be a link between the particular 1D numbers that we're going to ask to be admitted in the bar table and the objects on the map, but if you think that's enough for the purposes -- I'm telling you what our purpose is. If you think it's enough and it won't be a problem later when we make a bar table motion, we'll do it that way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Just tell us the number of the paragraphs you are referring to as a -- by way of example.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: 29, 32, and I think 35 is the third one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not still persuaded why Mr. Karadzic needs to show these paragraphs to the witness. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I obviously leave most of this to Ms. Edgerton, but I need to repeat to the Court what I said to Mr. Robinson when he first indicated to us that -- well, at -- just before this witness was to testify, that they would be using a map. I told him at that time that that -- I didn't know exactly how they intended to use it, but it appeared to be a transparent and obvious attempt to circumvent the Trial Chamber's order. Now it's not only transparent, in my submission, but it's admitted. This is merely an attempt to get around the Trial Chamber's order in a way that not only undermines the spirit of the order, but it -- and, in fact, frankly, the letter of the order, but also provides the Chamber with much less information than it was seeking when it made the order in the first place, that these documents and the testimony be led live. So Ms. Edgerton may want to address more detailed aspects of this, but this is -- this is exactly what we were concerned it might turn out to be and now it's acknowledged as such explicitly by Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, your order was that we not have all these documents be associated exhibits because it was burdensome to the Chamber to review 230 documents as associated exhibits. So based on that advice, we decided to try to present it by way of this map. But now that the accuracy of the map has been questioned, we think that it's fair that the documents themselves be admitted and the Chamber can see then for itself at the -- during its deliberations exactly what the military -- legitimate military targets in Sarajevo were. So we don't see that this is circumventing your ruling, but we think that it's actually implementing it in the same way that the witness is here to be questioned about the reliability and provenance of the documents. And he's been -- that has happened. And so we want to make sure that there's an adequate basis for you to admit these from the bar table, that's the purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a -- whether to admit those documents through a bar table motion is a separate matter, a matter that the Chamber will deal with when it arises. However, still I do not see the point why Mr. Karadzic has to show this paragraph 29, et cetera, to the witness. If necessary, he can deal with it one by one, as ordered by the Chamber. And I expected that he would have done it during his direct examination, but it -- after being challenged, he may deal with point by point through the map and the documents relevant to those locations if necessary. But showing this paragraph in lump sum does not serve any purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, the problem is that it -- within the time that it would take for him to go through these documents one by one, we could call about 20 witnesses. And it's our estimation that it's not worth it for us to waste -- spend that kind of time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's your strategy -- it's up to the Defence what strategy it should take.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, then, the problem is that the Chamber is going to be deprived of information that it ought to have. So if the Chamber believes that these documents should be led one by one, we would like to ask the Chamber to give us an additional four hours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- to the total of 300.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it's out of the point. 300 hours is more than sufficient. It is the -- the Chamber is of the view that it is sufficient enough, and I will consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber sees no reason to change its position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. We'll make the motion for the bar table and see how it turns out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, sir, let me ask you this specifically. By looking at the documents, were you able to determine that this feature was used as a military object?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we established that without any uncertainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I asked whether you established or not, and tell us this: What about the Kosevo Hospital, how reliable are the documents on the abuse of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, just a second. How does it arise from the line of cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was challenged here, the map was challenged, the sources, the grounds, they were all challenged, and I intend to proffer these documents later on, and I would like to hear from the witness here whether the positions that are mentioned here that we have documents for, whether they are accurate and whether this was checked. And my question was misinterpreted. It sounds as a leading question the way it's worded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your specific question about the location or -- of Kosevo Hospital is not arising from the cross-examination. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please call up the map that was shown yesterday in relation to Bjelave and it had to do with Cekalusa Street. Could we have someone's assistance here, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, 6186, exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, sir, can you tell us what Bjelave is, is that a street or what?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Bjelave is a neighbourhood, it is a settlement, a part of town. It comprises a number of streets. There is a police club there, a special police unit, and so on. So it was helpful to show it in Bjelave as a settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, if we go from here westward, what is the next neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Ciglane, or rather, Mejtas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's to the south but if you go to the west?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ciglane.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see Cekalusa Street there? We see the Gabelina-Cekalusa Street there. You can also see the mosque. It runs parallel to where it says "Ciglane" and it's on the Bjelave side. Close to numbers 42 and 57, can you see it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the usher kindly put the cursor on --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, yes, yes. Yes. Yes, yes. I can see the street, Cekalusa Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you see the green spaces down there?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To which settlement does Cekalusa belong of the two, Ciglane or Bjelave?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as that is concerned, judging by the names of the settlements here, it's closer to Ciglane.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And judging by the geographic configuration?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as this here divides it, then it belongs here to Bjelave, or, rather, to Mejtas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just another question, Lieutenant-Colonel. You said yesterday that the map is not detailed enough. Are there any remaining positions and how many which have not been recorded on this map and it's been verified that they existed?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- that's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic has asked a very leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I think that's the question you put in -- during your direct examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. All right. Thank you. Just another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How long has your military career been?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 32 years of pensionable service or actually 35, if we take everything into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How long did you command mortars of all the time and in which period of your career?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I commanded the mortars in the first four years when I was the platoon commander, that is to say, up until 1972, and otherwise, when you work with them once you never forget it, the effects and the other thing and so on. It's a very interesting weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Just one more question, please. You were asked about corrections on page 5 today. As for adjustment, fire adjustment, can you use the fire adjustment for one weapon for firing from another weapon and from a distant position?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, if you fire from a group of mortars, four or five, depends on how many because it depends on the specific unit, then you make the fire adjustments from one weapon and the other weapons follow the elements. And then the elements are changed, the angle, the distance, and so on. So once the fire adjustment is made for one weapon and if the result is positive, then you can move on to a group fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And can information from azimuth 240 be used from weapons which are on the 170 azimuth?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Where does anything -- first of all, I didn't ask a single question today about corrections, and where does anything about azimuths arise from the cross-examination at any point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You asked the question with respect to the distance from the original target, and during the course of answering the question he talked about the adjustment. I will ask my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber agrees with Ms. Edgerton. Move on to another topic, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then the question would be, Lieutenant-Colonel, whether during the war you were mostly an intelligence and security officer except for this one period?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, throughout the war and during the half year that I spent as the battalion commander, I did not neglect my basic duty because I was in charge of intelligence and security issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Lieutenant-Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Mr. Sarenac, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djuric. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Before your commence your evidence, Mr. Djuric, I must draw your attention to a certain rule that we have at this International Tribunal, that is, Rule 90(E) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, Mr. Djuric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Djuric.

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As you hail from civilian authorities, I will not address you by a rank though I believe you held a rank in the police?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I held the rank of lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you -- and before that I will ask you just to express my warning in accordance with Rule 90, I will just warn you that we should make pauses between sentences and we should also speak as slow as possible so that everything would be recorded.

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you give a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was quite fast. If you can just wait for a second and make a pause.

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I gave a statement to the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see 1D7826 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do not be confused by the redactions. By decision of the Trial Chamber it was assessed that some parts were irrelevant, so just neglect that. And taking that into account, can you see your statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read and signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: I read it and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please show the last page to the witness so that he could identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this statement one that truthfully conveys what you told the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to ask you the same questions today, would your answers substantially be the same as in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. My answers would substantially be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this package to be admitted in accordance with the 92 ter rule, but there are several documents that Mr. Djuric was kind enough to bring here himself and I would ask him about them viva voce.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, first of all, I notice that the redactions on the B/C/S version of the statement are not very effective and I'm going to tell our Case Manager to replace that so that the document is more -- is better redacted. Secondly, we're offering four associated exhibits. We're asking that each of them be added to the 65 ter list because we didn't have them at the time that lists were filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As regards paragraph 44, Mr. Karadzic, of this witness which refers to a killing of Muslims, death of Muslims, in Drum, I'm not sure whether it refers to the killing in the indictment because the indictment refers to the time-frame of June but the witness is talking about something in April. So I would like to deal with the issue with the witness and how he came to know the incident as well. Otherwise, we'll admit the statement as well as other -- the four associated exhibits. Shall we give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The 92 ter statement 1D7826 will be Exhibit D3093, and the four associated exhibits will be Exhibits D3094 through D3097 respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will read the summary of Mr. Djuric's statement in the English language. [In English] Mane Djuric was the acting chief of the SJB Vlasenica and became the chief of the same SJB in August 1992. Also he was a member of the Crisis Staff of Vlasenica municipality throughout 1992. Mane Djuric believes that in Vlasenica the population was roughly half Serbian and half Muslim with very few Croats. Approximately the same proportions were applied at the Vlasenica SJB after the multi-party elections. However, competence was not taken into account when appointments were made. The relationship between Muslims and Serbs in Vlasenica was quite good; however, this began to change after the multi-party elections. When the Muslims and Croats proclaimed a sovereign BH, the Serbian people realised that sovereignty was established against their will and that none of their requests would be granted because they would be out-voted. The Serbs looked for a way to protect themselves, and so the idea of regional association in the Serbian autonomous regions was created and autonomous regions of Birac was established. The Crisis Staff was established in early April 1992. Mane Djuric considers it was common practice for the municipal authorities to establish a Crisis Staff when people's lives or property were threatened. As a joint Assembly in Vlasenica did not function and the security situation deteriorated by the hour, it was decided that a Crisis Staff be established to monitor and take measures to overcome the situation. The Crisis Staff were not always able to consult the SJB chief Sarajevo because the -- CJB, CJB chief of Sarajevo because at the beginning the telephone lines were down and the road to Sarajevo was not passable. Very soon after the Crisis Staff's creation, a decision was made to divide Vlasenica municipality into three. Many of the Crisis Staff members left Vlasenica for the municipality of Milici and therefore the Crisis Staff could not function. Following this, boards of commissioners were established to better inform the Presidency of the Republika Srpska what the situation was in the municipalities. By 19th of April, 1992, a large number of Muslims and Serbs had left the area, and the Crisis Staff of Vlasenica declared an imminent threat of war due to the impossibility of convening the municipal Assembly. The departure of the Muslim citizens, the damaged interethnic relations, and the large number of illegal weapons held by civilians. Further, a decision was adopted taking over power in Vlasenica as the joint Assembly could not function. On 21st of April, 1992, the Vlasenica Territorial Defence was mobilised because the property in public and socially owned enterprises were threatened. Many employees remained at home and looting of the buildings had begun. There was no fighting or armed resistance in Vlasenica on that day. It was common knowledge that both Muslims and Serbs were obtaining arms before the outbreak of the war. The Serbs acquired most of their weapons legally by being mobilised in the Territorial Defence. However, the Muslims acquired most of their weapons illegally through the SDA party. Although, the SJB knew this was occurring, it was very difficult for the police to seize the weapons due to the mixed police patrols. An attempt was made to disarm citizens who possessed illegal weapons. A number of weapons were handed over; however, not all of the Muslims co-operated. Intelligence was gathered and interviews were conducted with them. Those who did not hand over their weapons had criminal reports filed on them. Further, a decision was made by the Crisis Staff to disarm all active reserve members of the police force as the citizens no longer trusted the joint police because it could not guarantee safety due to its composition. The decision to disarm all of the reserve police was made by the Crisis Staff alone without any orders from higher authorities. After this a number of Muslim men did not return to the police station for work. This decision was not an attempt to get rid of the Muslims in the police. Nobody was given a decision on termination of employment. The Muslims decided of their own accord not to become -- to come to work again. Mane Djuric recalls that an Intervention Platoon from the army caused problems in Vlasenica and that reports were filed against them, and in some cases they resisted the police. It was proposed that this unit be put under the control of the police; however, this was unsuccessful. Therefore, an order was given for all paramilitary units were disbanded and action was taken against those who broke the law. A procedure was established for those citizens who wished to leave Vlasenica to ensure that they were not being forced out of the territory. Civilians could not leave until they signed a document saying that they would leave the municipality voluntarily. This applied both to the Muslims and to the Serbs. Many Muslims wanted to leave town; however, many did not have their own transportation and therefore they assembled in the front of the municipal buildings and asked for transportation to be provided by the authorities. At the same time, many Serbs came to Vlasenica as they had been forced to leave their homes by Muslims and travelled to Vlasenica from neighbouring municipalities. Mane Djuric denies that there was a camp for Muslims in Vlasenica as alleged. He was aware that there was a holding centre for Muslims, Croats, and Serbs who wanted transportation and shelter. Some people went voluntarily in the evenings to spend the night in the centre before returning to their own homes in the morning. Serbs wanted accommodation -- wanting accommodation were accommodated in a building centre in Susica which was secured by the Territorial Defence and the VRS. Mane Djuric was aware that before the outbreak of the armed conflict the Muslims were establishing their own armed forces because they planned to wage a war to create a sovereign Islamic BH. By mid-1991 they had established the Patriotic League and the Green Berets in Vlasenica. The Muslims also used the reserve police force as Muslims were in the majority in this organisation. Mane Djuric attended a meeting at which Radovan Karadzic and at this Karadzic supported the implementation of the law advocating -- advocated helping the Muslims and Croats. Mane Djuric never heard of any Vlasenica municipal officials say that Radovan Karadzic issued an order regarding Muslims that could be threaten lives -- their lives or property. Further, Mane Djuric considers that the Serbian army did not conquer any territory, merely liberated what had been occupied by the Muslims. [Interpretation] I see the time. Would you like me to continue with other documents or should we rather do that after the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the planning purpose, I'm thinking about having two 30-minute breaks, and if a further extension is necessary taking a break of 15 minutes if there's -- I will -- I asked around so we'll be able to know whether it's feasible. We'll take a break for half an hour and resume three to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning, Your Honours. Just a couple things before Mr. Karadzic starts. One, I won't go into it, but at page 28, line 9, there's an incorrect statement by Mr. Karadzic about the redaction. I don't think the Trial Chamber found anything irrelevant in ordering it redacted. I won't go further than that. Two, when Mr. Karadzic leads the additional documents live, I'd request that he lead and just tell us where, when, and how Mr. Djuric got these documents which he brought so that that doesn't come out of my time, that basic foundation. Third, my understanding from the Defence witness calendar they provide us is that Mr. Djuric arrived in The Hague last Saturday. Now, the revised transcript has 13 new paragraphs where they went over adjudicated facts with the witness and got new comments on them. So I don't see why when he brings documents with him it can't be done what the Prosecution always does, which is to include these in a revised statement or give us a proofing note or something. He complains about the amount of time he has. He's got to lead this stuff live because he didn't bother to incorporate it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The reason it wasn't incorporated in the statement is because we don't have -- we didn't have enough time to get the documents translated. And since you don't accept associated exhibits of untranslated documents we didn't put it in the statement. Mr. Nicholls is correct, we should give a proofing note when we receive the documents and some explanations of what their relevance are and we'll try to do that in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I wouldn't like to spoil the concord between Mr. Nicholls and Mr. Robinson, but Mr. Nicholls hasn't spent a day in detention and I have to conduct my defence from the Detention Unit, thus meeting the witnesses only once they have arrived --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's an inappropriate comment. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was supposed to be a joke, Your Excellency. I don't know whether I managed to convey it but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djuric, do you have your statement before you in hard copy?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, may the witness rely on his statement on a hard copy before him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yeah, if necessary you may refer -- you may consult with your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djuric, kindly go to paragraph 44 of your statement in order to shed some light on certain things. It says: "I do know that people were killed on both sides in the fighting in the Muslim villages of Pliskavice, Drum, Gradina, et cetera ..." When you say that they were killed sometime later, what does it refer to?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: The first activity was on the side of the Territorial Defence in early May. The next operation or activity was jointly with the army sometime in June. As far as I know, in the previous activities there were no casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So on the 21st of April -- well, the victims on both sides at the three locations, that does not refer to the 21st of April; correct?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: No, it does not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, is it clearer now what paragraph 44 refers to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would like to hear what the witness knows about Drum. Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Drum village is in the immediate environs of Vlasenica municipality. It's actually a town settlement basically where both Serbs and Muslims lived together. It was typical of Drum that in early -- in April, a group was registered there manning check-points headed by Ferid Hodzic, the then TO chief who separated the TO and he was appointed in legitimate fashion by the joint Municipal Assembly of Vlasenica. One could hear shots fired and provocations from the direction of those barricades aimed at Vlasenica itself because the distance is quite small.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What I meant was the Muslims -- death of Muslims you referred to in your statement, your statement says: "I heard about the death of the Muslims in Drum village from a Muslim who lived there ..." Do you remember that? Could you expand what happened and what you heard and who it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That event took place in early June, perhaps on the 2nd or 3rd of June. There was an operation, so to speak, conducted by the TO and parts of the JNA where there were between eight and nine casualties that I found out about. The next day when a certain Begic arrived, a Muslim from that village whom I had known before because he worked in the forestry company which dealt with cutting wood, he came and wanted to ask that the victims be buried properly. He said that he trusted the police, and indeed we met his request and made sure that the victims were buried properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I will leave it at that. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't think everything was recorded. Can you tell us, you said that from Drum they were firing towards the settlement of Vlasenica itself. Can you clarify? What kind of shooting was that and was that the reason for the intervention?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: I've mentioned the reasons for the intervention. There was information that there were larger quantities of illegal weapons provided by Mr. Ferid Hodzic. He also manned the check-point there because beyond Vlasenica and Drum there is Cikote, which is a Serb village, and people had difficulty passing through. They complained about it a lot. Sometime during early evening hours, one could also hear and see shots being fired, especially with tracing bullets, towards Vlasenica which is in the part of town which is called Panorama. Such provocations occurred practically daily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there anything of military nature in Panorama, the part that was being fired at?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: No, it's a civilian part of town, it's a settlement which -- where the Panorama Hotel is as well as an additional 11 apartment blocks called by the same name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Karadzic kindly pause and repeat his question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Because of overlapping, you were not heard, Mr. Karadzic. Could you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question was whether in the Panorama Hotel there was some kind of command?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: At the time in the Panorama Hotel there was no command. The hotel functioned as such, and later on a unit was billeted there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's have a look at the documents you were so kind to provide.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 0 -- 1D07843.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where did you get this document, Mr. Djuric?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: This document and some others that may appear later is something that I did not directly participate in, in the events they concern. I found them or actually was given them during the hand-over of duty between myself and my previous colleague Radomir Bjelanovic at the police station. They were kept in our archives in a safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me read it out. It says: "Subject. "Request to suspend decision on the joining of Vlasenica municipality to become part of the Autonomous Region of Birac." Can we go to page 2, the last page, to see who signed it. The date is the 17th of January, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who signed it and what is this document?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: The signature is that of the president of the Executive Council, Izet Redzic who at the time was the president of the Executive Board which was lawfully appointed by the joint Vlasenica Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is this decision about? Can we go back to page 1? This is not a Serb autonomous region. It was called the autonomous region; correct?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Redzic was objecting to Vlasenica municipality joining the Autonomous Region of Birac. The goal of that entity was to remain part of Yugoslavia and Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what was that -- what was that he objected against and what was he asking for?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Probably as a representative of the most numerous party in the Assembly, the SDA, he put in their objection, they were opposed to this joining. It wasn't their intention --it wasn't the purpose of it to create independent regions as such, but to preserve the unity of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Yugoslavia. It states explicitly that he had been provided with instructions or advised on a certain strategy that ran contrary to the preservation of either Bosnia-Herzegovina or Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it say here that out of the 60 deputies, 27 were members of the SDS, 26 of SDA, and then there was another leftist party? But the ethnic make-up was in total 31 Serb deputies and 29 Muslim deputies, taking into account the leftist parties as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The decision was passed by most of the votes of the Serb deputies as well as most of the political parties; correct?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Karadzic kindly wait and repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It didn't make its way into the transcript. What was their reaction? What did they ask for and why?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: They asked that this decision be suspended by virtue of this document, and during the session the SDA deputies walked out of the Assembly, whereas the representatives of the leftist parties of Muslim ethnicity abstained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go to the next page -- actually, this is what I wanted. Do you recall some similar situations to this one from the joint Assembly? Was there any voting in the joint Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes. That situation kept recurring whenever out-voting took place in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3098, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 1D07844 next. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is this document of the 30th of March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: This document is an assertion really that before a military court there were proceedings against Izet Redzic for obstruction and take-over of military documentation by the military organs on the 30th of March, 1992. It was prevented that the documentation be taken over, although the persons who were supposed to seize it were authorised to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'll read out the last part. "Before a military court in Sarajevo there are proceedings that were instituted against Izet Redzic ..." et cetera, et cetera. And the last sentence says: "The aforementioned person is charged with criminal offences pertaining to Article 205, paras 1 and 3 ..." I'll repeat it slowly: "The aforementioned person is charged with offences from Article 205, paragraphs 1 and 3 of the penal code of the SFRY." So it was a criminal offence; correct?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this admitted and MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you say that -- this is related to the proceedings against Izet Redzic for obstruction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And signed by Izet Redzic himself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, because he was the president of the Executive Board and it was probably that body which asked that the register of documents be forwarded, and by sheer coincidence he was one of the people involved. He was authorised to sign documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3099, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 1D07845. The next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djuric, kindly introduce this document to us dated the 24th of April, 1992. Who was writing to who and ordering what?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: This is a TO document by the TO commander, whereby they are making a security assessment in the territory of Vlasenica municipality, with a particular stress on the possession of illegal weapons. Based on their knowledge, they created this assessment and found it necessary to secure preconditions to have the weapons handed over, seized, or returned to the competent authorities or, to be more specific, to have the weapons placed in the public security station in Vlasenica because the public security station was competent to keep registers of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us something, what village does the first order refer to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, no objection, just for the record in case it matters later, I think the date is 27 April, not 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I note it consists of several documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please tell us, in addition to Turalici - can we see the next page? - what other locations does this document relate to?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Well, the villages in the Vlasenica municipality. Some are hamlets, some are local communes. Among others, we see Turalici, Halihodzici, Zekici, Beros. Then in the next document, Kujancici, Gramdzici [phoen]. Then in the next document, Donji Sadici, Dragasi, Mramor. In the next document, Hrastovac, Sehmanovici [phoen], Bajica Brdo [phoen], Dzemat. In the next we see Gradina. So these are the places, settled-up areas where the Territorial Defence and the security organ, when they conducted the assessment, learned that there was a large quantity of illegal weapons. Most of these were automatic weapons. And to that end, an order was issued to these local units to engage in seizing these weapons, to take activities to seize them, to be very careful and do it in a peaceful way without any casualties and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In lines 2, 4, 6, 8, it says: "For the purpose of seizing weapons from citizens in a peaceful manner without applying repressive measures except in the cases where extremists opposed the implementation of this task." And then a little lower, under 4, it says: "Fire should only be opened in the event that our forces are attacked by extremists." Now, is this or was this successfully carried out in this manner without having to open fire?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: For the most part, members of these activities complied with this order, and as far as I know, in all of these activities there were no casualties or any major issues. However, there was this problem of old weapons being handed in for the most part, whereas the illegally obtained weapons, automatic weapons, were not really handed in because a number of extremists continued to conceal those weapons. So that we could see in the evening at the station that a lot of old weapons were handed in and very few automatic rifles, and -- but we did have the information from the field to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you just tell us whether the wording or the substance of this -- the text is identical or very similar except that it relates to different villages?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, except that it relates to various villages and different times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were aware on negotiations on the establishment of three municipalities in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. I was apprised of it. I knew that these activities were under way, that there was talk about dividing the Vlasenica municipality into three municipalities. There was a decision taken by the Assembly, a joint Assembly, in other words, a decision taken by all deputies that the municipality should be divided into three municipalities - the Serbian municipality of Vlasenica, the Muslim municipality of Vlasenica, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter kindly requests that the witness repeat the third name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. You spoke a bit too fast, so interpreters could not hear the name of the third municipality and could you repeat from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. So at this multi-ethnic Assembly a decision was taken to divide the municipality of Vlasenica into three: The Muslim, the Serb municipality of Vlasenica, and the Milici municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That suffices for now. Could you tell the Trial Chamber -- could you list a number of places that would enter the Muslim municipality of Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Well, one of the largest places was the Cerska village, and then all the villages that were mentioned earlier in this document, they were also envisaged as part of the Muslim municipality of Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you demand that Cerska be disarmed?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.
