The Territorial Defence made an assessment on the disarming of Cerska; however, that activity was not carried out then because there was a large concentration of personnel there, a large number of able-bodied men and armed men, so that the decision was taken not to carry out that action then but, rather, to try to accomplish this through negotiations. However, that did not -- that was not successful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Albeit belated, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Two things, Your Honour, one objection to leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The right way to ask that, in my humble submission, would be something like: What was the policy or attitude towards Cerska and disarmament? The second is that although he has shown these documents which the witness brought, this is a topic, division of the municipality into three different entities, that easily could have been included in the statement. So he's now moving on to a new area that we really haven't had - unless I'm missing it in the statement - notice of and using the documents as a vehicle to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you follow, Mr. Karadzic? And please don't forget Mr. Nicholls' request, which the Chamber endorsed, that you lead the witness as to the provenance of the document, i.e., where, when, and how this witness got those documents. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. This witness was a police officer. He did not take part in the negotiations but he was aware of them. However, when we discussed this issue of disarming and the toleration of these things in Cerska, I had to ask him about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djuric, could you please tell us how did you obtain all these documents? Did you obtain them in the same way, all of them?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Well, as I said a moment ago, I actually got these documents during the hand-over of duties, I got them from my predecessor, the chief Radomir Bjelanovic at the Public Security Station Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender the previous document for identification as a single document because it consists of a number of different documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are they -- were they written all by a same person? Because some documents were cut off in the bottom part so we cannot see them all in the scanned version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3100, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see 1D7846, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you obtained this document and what this document is about?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: This is a statement by a citizen, Fikret Muminovic. He gave this statement to the police station, or rather, public security station in Milici. He was -- he provided a statement, a clear statement, that on the 4th of April, 1992, he met Fadil Turkovic, who was the police station commander in Vlasenica, and on this occasion together with others he was issued a Schmeisser automatic rifle and some ammunition. However, in the following days he handed over that weapon at the public security station in Milici. He said that he had received it from Fadil Turkovic, the then-commander of the public security station. So we can see here that even Fadil, as a commander, as an official, a police official, was involved in the illegal arming and distribution of weapons to Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document, please, for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, on two counts. I didn't object but that was an extremely leading way to answer -- to ask the question. He could have simply asked: Do you know about the men in these documents? Was there any criminal activity you know of regarding them? Instead of having him read out the statement. Second, it's a statement, a verbatim statement, and it should not be admitted through this witness. They should call the declarant if they want to put in this statement and go through the ordinary established method, which has been discussed here many times, of putting statements in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it's nice to hear Mr. Nicholls saying that -- been saying that since the beginning, but the rule the Chamber has applied is that contemporaneous statements that are confirmed by the witness can be admitted. And so the witness has confirmed this statement, and therefore it should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second -- no, no, just a second --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may add, this is of the nature of an official note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry to rise, Mr. President, but there are at least two previous occasions when I came as -- as either in the capacity of the lawyer calling the witness or in anticipation of just such a moment, armed with all the jurisprudence and the case practice in this particular case with regard to these materials, but did not on this occasion because this matter has been ruled on repeatedly by the Trial Chamber as I advised Mr. Robinson just a few moments ago before we started court and for which he did not have a response. This falls within the lex specialis, as the Court ruled in a precisely analogous situation before, not too long ago. And these are -- kind of by pretending not to acknowledge the repeated decisions of the Chamber on this matter and others, we find ourselves dealing with unacknowledged motions for reconsideration repeatedly. But this should be a simple one. My best recollection is the Court dealt with this in the very recent past in just the way I've described. There aren't that many bright-line tests in the law or in this case, but this has certainly been one of them that the Court has applied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this an official note or a statement? Mr. Djuric, could you read out the title.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The title here is "Statement." It was provided to authorised officials, in other words, to police officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to add anything, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm having trouble recalling the decisions that Mr. Tieger has been alluding to. I don't think this is lex specialis because it wasn't taken by the Office of the Prosecutor or the Defence for the purposes of this litigation which would require it to be tendered under 92 bis. So unless he's remembering something that I just have simply forgot -- my understanding of the Chamber's practice is that you've admitted statements of third parties, even un -- non-contemporaneous ones, where the witness has confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Lex specialis -- the lex --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, unless you have something urgent, I was thinking about the same so we'll put this under advisement and come back to this issue in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. I'm happy to provide the jurisprudence indicating lex specialis are statements taken for the purposes of criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that, but I wasn't clear whether we admitted this kind of statement, but we'll see. I'll leave it at that. Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the penultimate paragraph, could you please tell us what it says about the effect this has on others? What did this witness say about it? And whether the weapons in Zaklopaca were handed over?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Well, the situation in -- is becoming more and more dangerous from day-to-day for civilians --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Because the situation is becoming more and more dangerous for citizens from day-to-day, I will do the best I can personally that all those who possess illegal weapons in my village and in the wider area to hand them over so that life could return to normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, were the weapons from Zaklopaca handed in?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know they weren't; however, that was within the competence of another public security station so I can't really claim this. But I do know that not in a -- not in any village were the weapons handed in in their entirety, and so it was in Zaklopaca as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have tendered this but now I await your decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But please bear in mind, Mr. Karadzic, that without putting some foundational questions, just putting the document and asking the witness what this document is about, is a typical way of leading question. As objected to or indicated by Mr. Nicholls. So for the remainder of the document, please bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. But this was a document that the witness brought himself and that is why I asked him why he had brought it, how he had obtained it, and what they represent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that's the question you should put at the end of your question, but that does not offer you the excuse for putting leading questions, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Today you mentioned also - I'm not sure whether it was in the statement or verbally - paramilitaries and crimes of a unit which could not be placed under control. What was the situation as regards crimes? Who committed them and what was the attitude of the police station to this?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: From the very beginning and even earlier, there is paramilitary groups, or let me call them just paramilitaries, appeared. One of their goals was to commit crimes, or rather, to loot, steal, destroy property and the like. In the public security station within its possibilities at the time up until mid-May or thereabouts when stronger and more efficient control of functioning was established could not oppose those groups and para groups. Consequently we frequently came into conflict with them, but later on when the station was established, we settled accounts fiercely with these groups and paramilitaries. And by mid-August or thereabouts we managed to have the situation under control and they were no longer able to commit the acts which they used to commit in the area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D07841.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what this document is and who drew it up?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: This document is a response to a memo, a dispatch, requested by the chief of the security service in the Romanija Bircan [phoen] centre on the basis of the need to brief from the Ministry of the Interior. This is our or, rather, my response to the questions contained in this document. Inter alia, we are responding to the question concerning the existence of these paramilitaries units. We replied that the paramilitary units have not been registered in combat operations, but that they were noted for their crimes, inter alia, one para group, the so-called Red Berets, is mentioned. I can add that there was a group called Vukovarci, that means the men from Vukovar, and other similar groups that had no names at all. Their only goal was to loot and commit other crimes. As there was a question about co-ordinated action between the army and the Ministry of the Interior, we replied that we were engaged jointly with the then newly established military police of the Army of Republika Srpska in providing expert assistance so that these persons could be punished. We provided professional assistance along these lines, or rather, it was agreed at a meeting held later that as far as all members of the VRS were concerned, they should be prosecuted by the army and the civilians should be prosecuted by the public security station. So we gave maximum support to the army security organs in order to have these people placed under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened and how did you resolve the issue of civilians who were present in the combat operations zone?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: The civilians in the combat operation zone came to Vlasenica and, if possible, they immediately went to places they wanted to go to. The closest places were Kladanj, Olovo, some of them went in the direction of Tuzla, but all of them via Kladanj. As for those civilians who could not be transported to the desired place on that particular day were accommodated at one point in a Territorial Defence facility in Susica where they would spend the night. And on the following morning the activity would be continued, namely, they would go wherever they wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the Serb civilians leave also and where?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: The departure of civilians from Vlasenica was specific because it began as early as in February or March, so that some of the Muslims went in the direction of Tuzla and then later on returned. But the intensity of this movement increased immediately before and after the 21st of April. Generally the Muslims were going in the direction of Tuzla, that is to say, what is today the territory of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, whereas the Serbs mostly sent their families to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you report about this holding centre in Susica to your superior, that is to say, Mr. Cvijetic?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, whenever possible. However, the typical thing was that in terms of the territorial organisation of the Vlasenica municipality before the war it belonged to the Tuzla region, so that in the beginning when the power was down, it was difficult to send communication up until the time when the relays were redirected and until we found other sources of electricity. So we sent some dispatches by courier and then later on we resumed sending reports electronically once we had the electricity running again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please look at the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please read to us paragraph 3. But slowly, please. Read out the third paragraph "In the area ..."

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: "In the area of this public security station, one centre for taking care of persons from the combat operation zone has been registered. These persons are treated in accordance with the principles and rules established by international humanitarian organisations. The centre is under the jurisdiction of the Serbian army."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Which centre are you talking about here?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: This was precisely the reception centre in Susica, because it's undoubted, if you analyse it, that up until the 31st of May the centre was only of humanitarian character. All the persons who arrived there, arrived for the sole reason to be provided with transportation as soon as possible, because during the day it was not possible to provide so many vehicles and buses for all of them to be transported on the same day. So up until that period the character was only humanitarian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this please be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you are the author --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or can we, rather, move it up a little bit so that we can see who the author of the document is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes. This is a response to the dispatch from the chief of the security centre who collated the information arriving from all areas later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3101, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was the response to the questions from the next level, the security services centre, that is to say. Was it the usual practice, or rather, how did you inform each other, these questions between you and the security services centre?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: In the beginning, as I said, there were difficulties during the month of May and partly June as well because on the 24th of April, Vlasenica was left without electricity which lasted until March 1993. But as there are small power-plants in the territory of the municipality then we used them, but we had to prioritise who would be supplied with electricity, the hospital, for example, and the MUP. So the communications were maintained by courier. The driver would come along, he would pick up the mail, and then take it to them. And once the communications system was established, then we would use teleprinter dispatch or some of it by fax when that was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What sort of information was requested from the security services centre?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: The security services centre of Romanija and Birac mostly insisted on establishing the public security station as the institution. It came from the top, from the minister, that the institutions of the Ministry of the Interior are to be established and would work in accordance with the Law on Internal Affairs, that is to say, the requests regarding the security of citizens, the security of property and persons, traffic, the rights of citizens such as issuing ID cards and so on. So these were the most frequently mentioned information, and the insistence was on lawfulness and on removing from the Ministry of the Interior the persons who had committed crimes or had shown a tendency to commit crimes. And we were doing this continuously from the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have 1D07842. Thank you. Could we please zoom in so that the witness could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what was requested from you here and what your response was?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Information was requested once again about the existence of the reception centre. The response was that people were accommodated there for as short as possible, until the conditions were met for them to go to the areas where they wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who requested this from you?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Again it was the centre chief. Probably he had to respond to a dispatch from the minister or somebody else from the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Can you please tell us this. You responded to a question. Can you please re-tell us what the first and second paragraphs contain. The first and the third, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. In the first paragraph the substance is that in the territory of the Vlasenica municipality there was a reception centre for the accommodation of persons of both Muslim and Serbian ethnicity who expressed a wish to leave the territory of Vlasenica municipality as soon as possible up until the technical conditions for their departure were met, that is to say, buses provided and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which reception centre do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Also Susica --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the speakers please slow down for the purpose of interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Shall we start over again from your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what is said about the conditions in Susica in the third paragraph, but please speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: The reception centre meets all the criteria in terms of accommodation, food, and all the other provisions prescribed by international institutions and it is also in accordance with the decision of the organs of the Serbian republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And was this the line of reporting to the ministry and all the higher instances?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was a response to a question from the chief of the centre of public security because that was the subordination. He often received an order from the minister to draw up a report concerning his area. The minister would then collate such information for the needs of various institutions of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djuric.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness and I move to tender this document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3102, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Djuric, your evidence in this case, evidence in chief, has been admitted in most part in writing, i.e., through your statement and now -- in lieu of your oral testimony and now you'll be asked by Mr. Nicholls in his cross-examination. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djuric, we've met before, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go into private session for one moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: July 1995, your boss is Dragomir Vasic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: At that point you were deputy of the station in Zvornik, the MUP station, correct, that had authority over the region?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the security centre for the Birac region.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we quickly bring up 65 ter 24700. And go to e-court page 12 in the English, Serbian page 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is the security centre the one that is to be abbreviated as CSB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. CJB, the public security station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: SJB or CJB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] C stands for centre, J for javna or public, and B stands for security. The lower level would be SJB, public security station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was there a CSB in, for example, Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The public security centres --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Security services centres existed before the war when everything was under the same umbrella; however, during the war, the public security was split from state security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I'll leave it at that. So in the document we saw, in the previous document, in which you sent the report to the Sarajevo CSB, it was to the CSB, not CJB, at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I have to keep reaching ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Very quickly I just want to go through some call-signs that we talked about in our interview. The communications centre was -- in Zvornik CJB was Omega; correct ? You need to answer verbally. You nodded your head.

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Omega 1 is the chief. July 1995, that's Dragomir Vasic; right?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Omega 2, that's you?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Omega 21 is commander of the PJPs. July 1995, that is Danilo Zoljic; right?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Very quickly if we can go to English page 8, Serbian page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And while it's coming up, you'll probably remember Tomo Kovac is Tango 2, right? That's his sign? Deputy minister.

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document, either just these pages or -- I think it's a useful document. It's the Zvornik CJB call-signs for the whole centre. Whichever the Chamber feels is appropriate. It's about 57 pages in English, but it's just all the call-signs of the different people and units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson -- excuse me, Mr. President, we would like to just admit those pages that are referred to so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's fine. Perhaps the cover page, the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6188.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to ask you about a different topic now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could have P04937.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about the MUP's knowledge of the operation to take Srebrenica and the movement of the Muslim column, and we discussed this in our interview. Now P4937, when it comes up, is dated 12 July 1995. It's a report up the MUP chain to the ministry from the chief, Dragomir Vasic, showing that on the 12th of July, the MUP knew about Muslim soldiers trying to cross at Udrc, the need to block these Muslim soldiers from the column at Crni Vrh, who was leading them, that there's about 8.000 of them, about 1500 of them armed, and that they're in the Konjevic Polje-Sandici sector, and that this information was received from four captured Muslims. So basically, just can you confirm, this is a type of realtime relevant information that the MUP centre in Zvornik was receiving?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is a dispatch or a letter to the staff of police forces and the minister's cabinet. The situation was such that we had to report from one moment to the next so that they would be informed of what was going on. As for these assessments, sometimes they may have been approximate, other times correct. It all depended on what access to reliable information we had at any point of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sure. But my point is that it was important to Zvornik, and we all know about that later, I don't want to get into it now, but to be aware of the movement of the column of Muslim men from Srebrenica because there were soldiers in it and it could have been a threat to Zvornik; right?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 01932 , please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: While that's coming up, this is another dispatch from the chief of the centre, Dragomir Vasic, the next day, 13 July. It states in the beginning: "In the early morning hours of 13 July 1995 (at about 0400 hours), the first PJP ... had contact with a large enemy group in the Sandici and Konjevic Polje areas ..." There was a "fierce battle and the enemy suffered heavy losses. However," unfortunately for the Serbian -- Bosnian Serbian MUP, "Zeljko Ninkovic was killed ... and Nenad Andric, Zarko Zaric and Nenad Filipovic were wounded ..." You remember that incident, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: I recall this dispatch. Given the fact that I wasn't in that part which was closer to Bratunac, I focused most of my force and energy to protect Zvornik itself. Chief Vasic drafted this dispatch based on the relevant information he had. I'm sure of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. May I tender that, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6189, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just -- I can make this very quick so you may not have to give lengthy answers in the future about what you're doing. My understanding is that, as we can -- during this period, 11th to, say, 16 July, when we say there are mass executions of Muslim soldiers being committed by the MUP and the VRS, you're actually in the communications centre of the Zvornik Brigade most of the time. You're not out in the field; right?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't in the communications centre of the Zvornik Brigade. I was in the public security centre in my position as deputy, given the fact that Chief Vasic was away. Since he spent the -- several days in Bratunac. I was in MUP, in the seat of the public security centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You're right. I apologise. That was a bad misstatement by me. I'm normally dealing with VRS. That's what I meant to say, you were in the MUP centre, not in the field; correct? And you nodded your head so I think you agreed.

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Could I have 65 ter 24607, please. And start with just the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What I'm going to show you, sir, is a notebook or diary which I went through with you in Belgrade and which you confirmed at page 5 of your interview that it was your notebook and your handwriting. Do you remember this notebook?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Perhaps. In any case, I see it is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we have the original here if anybody needs to look at it. Could we go to page 9, please, of both versions. Now, Your Honours, just to be clear, what's in e-court is an excerpt. It's quite a large notebook. We don't have the whole thing in e-court and the whole thing isn't translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, I don't have really much time at all. I just want to go quickly, same exercise we did when I met you in Belgrade, talking about what these pages of your notebook show. This one we can see here, and we talked about it in your interview, was from the 11 July, you've got the date there, at a time when Predrag Blagojevic, body-guard for President Karadzic, apparently refuelled in Zvornik; correct?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Probably, since I noted it down, although I can't recall it off-the-cuff. Predrag Blagojevic, although I can't recall who the person was, but I can suppose he is as you say. I noted down that we issued him with 40 litres of diesel fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While you are asking, could I see the original version?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And below that we see Karisik came by and expressed an interest. And just quickly in our interview you told us that must have been Milenko Karisik; correct?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Most likely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we skip to page 11 now, moving quite quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now here, somewhat in line with the dispatches from Dragomir Vasic we saw on the 12th of July, the first one, we discussed in our interview how this was the 12th of July and where we see there Ravni Buljim, elevation 651, and then below it 651 circled, Bokcin Potok. Again, that was just information received about the movement of the column of Muslim men from Srebrenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Approximately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And at the bottom of the page, Sandici, Lolici, Kamenica, MUP, just locations of -- it's common knowledge now where the MUP was going to have to block the column on the road; correct?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: MUP forces were deployed, and that was my understanding at the time, to secure the road for the transport of civilians which were to travel along that route.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. On the 12th of July, the MUP, PJPs, and Borovcanin's special units were also blocking and capturing Muslim troops. I don't want to go through the documents again, but the one from 12 July we saw with Dragomir Vasic talked about the difficulties of fighting the Muslim soldiers and how they just captured four Muslim prisoners; correct?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: As I said, I can't be specific since I wasn't in that area. But I do believe that there were some problems as part of that communication. And if Chief Vasic reported it, I suppose it is correct or approximately correct to the best of his knowledge at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go to page 14 -- excuse me, 13 of the English, same in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right, yeah, very quickly. The bottom of the page here it says: "1 dead. "Nenad Andric. "Zarko Zaric. "Nenad Filipovic wounded." Those were the same people we saw in Vasic dispatch, 65 ter 01932, just a few minutes ago, that that took place early on the morning of the 13th; right?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's turn the page, page 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So the 14th of July now -- 13th of July, excuse me, 1995. And if you recall in our interview, that's page 28 of our interview, that the number there and the Deronjic was for Miroslav Deronjic in Bratunac, but you couldn't remember why his name was written there and what that contact was about; correct?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you don't remember today, do you?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: No. Perhaps I can add something, Your Honours. This note contains information as events developed as a reminder, and frequently I simply noted things down without any further clarification. At that point in time I may have been able to recall it, but it's much more difficult from this position here today. It's not a diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now go to page 16, English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Only one part I want to show you there is in the middle. It says Ljubisa for Krstic. We showed you the intercept I believe in our interview of Krstic, General Krstic and Ljubisa Borovcanin speaking on that day. So here, as you say, it's not a diary, but you've made a note that Ljubisa was looking for Krstic; correct? Borovcanin was looking for General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go to page 18. Very quickly there it's just a meeting held on 13 July at 1800 hours. Go to the next page, page 19 for the record in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So here we are in the evening of 13 July, and you've made notifications same day we saw Nenad -- Miroslav Deronjic's name in here of secure the buses, call regarding the buses' security, problem with buses and security, problem of Milici, security reinforced as an emergency. And in the interview we put it to you that that was about the buses filled with Muslim men, prisoners, who'd been captured and separated -- were separated at Potocari, who were being held in Bratunac, and we'll talk about the convoy in a minute. Was that what those notifications were about, security for the prisoners on those buses?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: No. I think the problem is the buses and securing the buses. It was asked that a certain number of buses be sent to Bratunac. One of the ways to communicate that was to use our communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, okay, but on the 13th of July the entire -- all the women and children are gone from Srebrenica. This is about buses in Bratunac; right?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, I'm through with that for a moment, although we'll probably come back to it if I have time. I'll ask you about something else that you discussed in our interview, that was at page 41, 65 ter is 24676. I'm not going to bring it up. But I asked you and you confirmed that you had no advance knowledge that on the 14th of July a column of trucks and buses from Bratunac carrying prisoners was going to arrive in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: No, I had no such knowledge whatsoever, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. Okay. However - and we'll go through it in a minute - you also made it very clear that you were at the Hotel Vidikovac in Divic, on the little bend that sticks out, near Zvornik, when that convoy of buses and trucks filled with Muslim prisoners arrived; correct?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Correct. I was in the Vidikovac Hotel and I could see the convoy from the terrace. It was around noon or a bit later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. And it was a surprise to you when you saw this huge convoy arrive; that's what you said?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So let me just get it clear. The chief of the centre, which you admitted earlier, Vasic, is in Bratunac on the 12th, 13th, and 14th, where the convoy leaves from. The deputy, the second from the centre, is in Zvornik, in communication and happens to be at the Vidikovac Hotel when the column arrives. So is your testimony that you in the MUP, you and Vasic, were able to track the movement of the Muslim columns through the wood, knowing what elevation they were at, knowing when they were in Sandici, knowing when they were in Lolici, knowing when they were in Kamenica, but you didn't know when your chief was in Bratunac that the Muslims were coming on the 13th to Zvornik? You lost track of all those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: What I said was indeed so. We did not have knowledge of the column moving to Zvornik. I cannot assert anything now, but I suppose that Chief Vasic was there, taking part in it, or that he may have had better knowledge of the movements of the convoy. If he had known that it was moving towards Zvornik, he would have probably informed me. I personally was unaware of it and I can't say anything positively about Chief Vasic. If he had known, he would definitely have informed me and provided suggestions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me correct the transcript. Unfortunately, I said 13th when it arrived. It's the 14th as we all know. That's not in dispute. I don't want to go into it at length but in an interview, which is 65 ter 22146, Tomo Kovac told us that when he saw you very late on the night of the 13th - this is at e-court pages 103 and 104 - that you told him that because there was not enough room in Bratunac, that the prisoners are to be transferred to Zvornik barracks, to Zvornik Brigade barracks. That's what Tomo Kovac said he learned from you before they arrived. Is that right or not right?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: It is true that I was in contact with Mr. Tomo, the minister or deputy, whatever he was at the time, and I told him that the column had reached Zvornik. I explained to him that we didn't know of their intentions as to which direction to take. We told him that it stopped but it was most likely to go on to the registered reception centre at Batkovic near Bijeljina or that the column would turn to Kalesija and Tuzla towards the demarcation line. However, events developed the way they did --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you --

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: What is the basic thing in all that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you. You may have missed the point of my question. He said that before - and to use our terminology, I'm not talking about the column of Muslim prisoners - the convoy of Muslim men in trucks and buses from Bratunac, he said that you told him before it arrived on the night of the 13th that the prisoners are to be transferred to Zvornik. Now, is that right what he said, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Only later, after arrival I informed Minister Kovac of the problem there. He provided certain suggestions. We thought they would go to Batkovic, as I've said, or to the demarcation line. And perhaps an hour or two later, after the conversation, he told me, "Keep the police out of it. There's the military police. You should only secure the road to allow for the traffic to go through."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, and that leads nicely to my next question which is why it's a bit surprising that you didn't know about this huge convoy of thousands of Muslim prisoners coming to your town from Bratunac, very close by, the day after you'd been in contact with Miroslav Deronjic, but there were - and there's lots of evidence in this case - MUP on those buses providing security. Milorad Bircakovic at P00360 testified unambiguously that on each bus there were four or five civilian police. He testified that he got on a bus -- I should say Milorad Bircakovic worked for Drago Nikolic - his security organ at the Zvornik Brigade - as his driver. He was ordered to get on a bus. That bus with civilian police on it went directly to Orahovac. KDZ407 was at Orahovac, completely separate testimony - that's P00379 - he's talked about receiving the prisoners who were brought in the school at Orahovac and how civilian police were escorting these prisoners in and helped them put the prisoners into the gym and those prisoners were then all killed. So how is it that the MUP, which is all your centre, come from Bratunac to Zvornik on the buses and then stay on the buses when they go to detention sites very near execution sites, and you don't know anything about it? That's a nice open-ended question for you.

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: I've already partially answered that question. When the column reached Zvornik it was stopped for a while. We didn't know what it was all about and what was going on. I asked for some answers from the minister. I informed him and I tried contacting the then-corps command Zivanovic, but communication was difficult to establish. After the second call to Minister Kovac, he suggested the following, "It is up to you to secure the road and I don't want to see any police meddling," which is what the police did. It secured that the convoy could keep going and, indeed, it did towards Zvornik. At that point in time I thought it was to go to Batkovic and Bijeljina or, perhaps, to turn to Karakaj and Kalesija, but it didn't take place. The only information I received from the police, from a police patrol, was that they turned somewhere in Pilica and somewhere else, but that they weren't allowed to go there. It was confirmed a number of times before and that's the truth of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Uh-huh. Okay. The execution site in Kozluk, on the 15th of July, the Trial Chamber have been there and seen how it's just straight -- a very short distance down a dirt road from the police station in Kozluk. And KDZ496, P00387 - I apologise for going so fast - testified at e-court pages 7 and 35 that there were men there in blue uniforms, police uniforms, as the executions took place. So again, I'm going to ask you -- well, first of all, when we met in Belgrade you agreed with me that those men on those buses and trucks did not go to Batkovic. They didn't go to Kladanj. They were virtually all executed. That's true, isn't it? You need to speak your answer.

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: If you allow me, I'd like to clarify something. The preceding days, perhaps even that day, the convoy was mostly moving via Vlasenica to Kladanj. We know that this convoy went in the direction of Zvornik; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Answer my question, please. Do you agree with me that all those men on the convoy that you met at the Vidikovac Hotel didn't go to Batkovic, didn't go to Kladanj, they were murdered?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: I only saw that later on, after about an hour or two, that the column stopped there, that they resumed, and then it -- I was informed that they were getting off the road, that they weren't -- that they were going to Kalesija, but I only had instructions that the police should just ensure and follow the routes along which this column was moving.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 4 - I would like to intervene in the transcript - the witness said: Only this one column -- convoy went to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Third time. Do you agree with me that all those men on the convoy, except for the odd survivor that escaped, that you met at the Hotel Vidikovac did not go to Batkovic camp; they were all murdered? Or do you think there's -- that's what you agreed with me in your interview. Are you now saying something different?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Well, I've said the same thing. It was our opinion that they would go to Batkovici; however, they didn't. But the knowledge about them moving and going in another direction and their execution, that was something that I only learned later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. When did you learn that they had been executed, all these men?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps on the following day or the following days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not sure if we're at break time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break. I think it's evident we cannot finish the next witness's evidence today. Is there any specific reason that we have to conclude his evidence today, Mr. Robinson, i.e., whether we cannot continue his evidence on Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We can continue his evidence on Monday. The problem -- he's been here since last Thursday because his testimony was delayed at the request of the Prosecution, so he's been here for a very long time, but as I understand it he can stay and, if that's necessary, we can do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll take a regular break for 45 minutes and see how it evolves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would just like to thank the Defence for accommodating us on that request regarding the next witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll break for 45 minutes and resume at 1.20. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.35 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My apologies for the delay. The Chamber had some discussions. Please continue, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could I have 24607 up again, please, page 19 in both languages. All right. This is just to orient us. This is a page we were looking at before from 13 July. Could we now go to the next page, 20 in each, please. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, sir, here in your handwriting we have on the top left "raid." Below that "4th Battalion." "741-016," "Tomo," and then an S or an 8 written under his name. Phone number 592-029 and "Popovic." Now, very quickly, you recall when we met that you told us this was, the Tomo and the phone number, that was Tomo Savic in Milici.

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, our position is this is 14 July 1995, because we've just moved on from pages which were 13 July, 14 July 1995 is the day of the executions of over a thousand men in Orahovac. Vujadin Popovic, Drina Corps security, is involved in those executions at Orahovac. The number 592-029 is the phone number of a little house right across the street from the Grbavci school which was used by the VRS. That the 4th Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade carried out executions in Orahovac that day and 4th -- and Orahovac is the area of the 4th Battalion. Now, when we spoke in Belgrade - and that's on page 45 to 46 of your interview - you told us that this could have been Vujadin Popovic but you didn't remember. You didn't know why you'd written down 4th Battalion and you didn't know why you'd written down that phone number. Do you stand by that or do you now remember why you have these entries in your book?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: I really don't remember and I couldn't comment on that. As I said, this is a note where something is recorded so that later one could -- but really, from this point in time, I do not remember what were the reasons for me to record this here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender this notebook. The portion we have in e-court is a total of 37 pages in English and Serbian original, either the entire thing because I think it's useful or, at a minimum, pages 9 to 21 which are the pages that I've gone -- or page 20, excuse me, are the pages I've gone over with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless indicated by -- otherwise indicated by the Defence, I prefer to admit pages 9 to 21. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, that's okay. We're going to probably talk about an entry on another page, but we could add it at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. What's the time-frame of those pages, Mr. Nicholls, pages 9 to 21?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 11 to 14 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll admit those pages and add, if necessary, later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I don't know if you want to just -- strike that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We give the number for this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6190, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 35025, please. And while it's coming up I will say this is a tactical intercept -- sorry, pages -- page 4 of the English and 12 of the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll not broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think we can broadcast this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you check? I was told that it is under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we upload it so that I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This might be a situation, Your Honour, where if we give it a different number that it can be broadcast without problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That on the left is not the right document. Page 12 of the B/C/S, please. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is an intercept and on the first page of the English -- sorry, page 4 of the English, we're only on page 1. That's right. Page 4 of the English we can see that this is talking about Friday, 14 July 1995. If we could skip to the next page of the English we could stay on the same page of the Serbian. Now, the first part I want to ask you about, sir, in this intercept is we've already established that you were Omega 2, that was your call-sign in July 1995. If you look down just at the sentence that begins "1930" about a quarter of the way down the page probably -- oh, no, sorry, sorry, I'm looking at the English. It's at the bottom of the page of yours, bottom quarter. It says: "1930 they organised and linked ambushes (Omega 02, Vuk)." Now, that's you talking to somebody named Vuk, who I don't know who that is, just about the movement of the armed Muslim soldiers, the column; right?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we look up a bit it says: "Omega 21 is in Pilica." That means Danilo Zoljic is in Pilica; right?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then if we look down we see: "Celik requested from Omega," which we saw was the Zvornik MUP communications centre, "to send security for Orahovac." Now, we already went through how buses that arrived from Bratunac on the 14th went to Orahovac, how there were MUP soldiers -- MUP policemen who went on those buses to Orahovac. We saw the entry in your notebook for 14 of July which had the phone number from Orahovac and Popovic. And here we see that somebody requested the MUP to send security for Orahovac. Does that refresh your memory about why you made these entries in your notebook that day?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: The handwriting here is not mine, so this is not my notebook. I cannot remember who could have been using my notepad.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is not your notebook, sir. This is an intercept from the Muslim side of intercepted conversations on the tactical lower ground level. But if it doesn't help you remember, it doesn't help you remember, but this is not your notebook. Don't worry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you ask the witness again whether he had such a conversation at 1930.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just again, you confirmed that at 1930 you had a conversation just about the armed Muslim soldiers who were threatening Zvornik, that that would be you.

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I -- when preparing for this part of my testimony in the Defence case I focused on 1992 in this case, so I didn't really study these transcripts a lot, and it often happens, as now, that I don't remember all the details. And I sincerely apologise, I will do my best to provide as accurate information as possible, but I cannot remember all the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender that document, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This page?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This page, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's already admitted according to my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It was MFI'd --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no -- I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Or not admitted actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it was not admitted at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: And I take it it may be for the same reason it shouldn't be admitted now if I'm thinking that this was not something that was testified to by one of the intercept operators because that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- I don't know whether or not this particular intercept has been authenticated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But this witness confirmed what he said about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That one line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Omega --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think that's enough, Your Honours. The reason it was not admitted previously in our bar table is that it was unfortunately, through our error, one of the ones where we didn't reference transcript pages and the 94 -- the prior admissions, it was previously admitted in Popovic, Tolimir, and I can't remember, either Krstic or Blagojevic. And we cited those prior admissions but we didn't cite them enough and Your Honours denied it on that basis. But as you said, it has now been authenticated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we -- it's fair enough to admit at least from "Omega 21" till "Orahovac."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's all you put to the witness .

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, the only other thing is the date is on the top which is important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Together with the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we give the number now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6191, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. 1992, you have -- your statement concerns that. You just said that's what you prepared for, and I want to talk to you about mosques being blown up in Vlasenica when you were there in August 1992 in the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, nobody was ever prosecuted and punished for this crime, blowing up the mosque; right?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: We instructed our service on the following day to conduct the on-site investigation; however, we submitted the report to the prosecutor's office. I don't know what happened with that later because those institutions were still not fully operational. And as none of us later asked for any additions nor was our report dismissed by any instance, and simultaneously the army was also allowed to conduct an investigation, this was what we carried out. We submitted our report about the on-site investigation to the prosecutor's office and that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, and so the answer then would be yes: To your knowledge, nobody was ever prosecuted and punished for this crime to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: No one has been prosecuted to this day; however, as I say, we submitted the report and the same measures, that is to say, the investigation could have been conducted by the crime police of the Army of Republika Srpska because there was an agreement that in case of criminal offences committed by members of the army should be prosecuted by the military organs. In such a case, if that happened, we would then contribute by forwarding the information we had to the relevant military organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Again, last time. I'm not asking you about the process, just to your knowledge, you don't know that anybody was ever actually punished for this crime, do you? That's a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: As far as I knew, I do not have information that anyone was prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement at paragraph 15 you talk about both sides, meaning Muslims and Serbs, arming and you talked about Serbs acquiring most of their weapons legally by being mobilised into the TO. Let's see if we can make this short. The SDS illegally armed Serb civilians, correct, in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it happened to a smaller extent because all members of armed forces according to the former law were assigned to specific posts and it was their duty to do that. Whoever responded to the lawful mobilisation could be issued by a soldier's equipment, including weapons. And I think that the SDS did not have any special need to be involved in illegal procurement of weapons because it was mostly the Serbs who responded to call-ups for mobilisation, that is to say, they reported themselves to the JNA and the TO. And obviously the Muslims refused this which can be found in a series of documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: -- that they refused to respond to the mobilisation, but they did obtain illegal weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: While it's coming up, you'll remember this document. It's your document, 3rd of August, 1992, to Romanija Birac CSB Sarajevo. And it discusses crimes dealt with by your police station. And it states: "In the period from 1st of April, 1992, to 30th of July, 1992" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "-- the Vlasenica public security station dealt with the following activities with regard to crime prevention," illegal possession of weapons, 108 cases; right?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Not boxes or cases, but cases in the sense of incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Correct. That's what I meant, 108 incidents, yeah. Okay. Now, P3216 is the crime register for your police station for 1992. I don't want to spend the time to bring it up, but do you recall that you previously had a chance to go through this crime register and you confirmed that through the end of July, the SJB processed 108 illegal weapons cases and there was not a single one of them where the person prosecuted was of Serb ethnicity, that it was only Muslims who were prosecuted for illegal possession of weapons; correct?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And going through that record, you also didn't find a single case of a crime committed by one of your police officers against a Muslim or Croat and it would have been there if it had been reported; right?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: The report says: Murder, five cases. I think these were, though I can't remember exactly now, acts done against life and limb of certain persons. Now I don't know, probably some of the cases that were under procedure were also those where the perpetrators were Bosniaks by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go into private session very briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, in paragraphs 23 to 26 of your statement you discuss the decision of 19 April 1992 of the Crisis Staff to disarm the police. And you say at paragraph 23 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let's bring that up. It's P06138.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Go ahead and look at your statement if you want to. You say in paragraph 23: "The Crisis Staff adopted this decision because the citizens no longer trusted the joint police force since it could not guarantee safety." At paragraph 24 you said: "After the decision to disarm the police was adopted, all SJB employees who had long-barrelled weapons were told ..." I'll skip a bit "... to bring the weapons to the station." And you also claim in paragraph 26: "It is not true that this was an attempt to get rid of the Muslims in the police and change the ethnic make-up of the police." Do you stand by that, paragraph 26, "this was not an attempt to change the ethnic make-up of the police"?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I stand by it. If I may, I'd like to clarify shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given that a decision had been made on the division of the municipality into the Muslim municipality of Vlasenica, the Serb municipality of Vlasenica, and Milici municipality, the policemen from the Milici municipal part went to Milici itself. And by protocol which was decided on at the Assembly concerning the division of the municipality also contained the following, it was stated that all of the three municipalities should begin with establishing their own institutions. In that case, Milici municipality started establishing their own institutions and the Serb municipality did the same later on when it was proclaimed. However, the Muslim side did not begin establishing institutions of their own for reasons that were known to them. It was a strategy of theirs because I could find in certain documents that Mr. Redzic stated he had signed it because he had received instructions from the SDA and Alija Izetbegovic to sign and to obstruct the process as long as possible in order to have as many people move out as possible. So the decision was to establish a police station which could be operational. Basically, at that point in time it did not exist. It did exist, but it was divided in terms of personnel. Some went to Milici, some Muslims had left even before the 21st of April because they left Vlasenica, and a very small number remained in the station. The reason for this decision so was to set up a new principle in order to establish a functioning police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now. --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go into private session briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm nearly done, Your Honours. I think I'm right at my time about. I'm going to have to speed up a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The special purpose unit you discuss in your statement at paragraphs 31 to 38 was under the command of Miroslav Kraljevic and you've previously said that it comprised 20 to 25 men. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And Elvis Djuric was the deputy; right? It's in your statement at paragraph 33?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's see if we can make this quick. That special unit was paid by the MUP and you actually signed the payrolls; correct?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you also talk about in your statement how from day one there were complaints with this unit. Paragraph 34 you talk about how this unit of 20 to 25 men mistreated Muslims. You also talked about how this unit made Muslims "disappear" without a trace. Paragraph 35 of your statement: "Every day I informed the Crisis Staff and the municipal leadership about the problems with this unit, but we had no solution. Armed fighting between the Serbs and the Muslims started on the ground, people were getting killed, and so we had no time to control this unit. Reports started coming in to the effect that on their own initiative they had started to take away Muslims from their homes and that these people then disappeared without a trace." Now this --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can we go in private session, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's paragraph 38 of your statement what we were just talking about where you say: Within a very short period you received an order, 27 July 1992. Sorry, based on an order of 27 July 1992, and you said: "As soon as we received this order, we disbanded the unit," the special unit run by Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now I'd like to look attendant 65 ter 18358.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This was not included in your statement although it relates to the documents about disbanding the unit and paramilitaries in your statement. Take a look at it. First of all, that's your signature on the bottom; right? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is a 10th of August, 1992, RE, topic, disbanding of the special unit formed during the war in the SJB. And you reference the 28 July and 27 July decisions to disband paramilitaries. And you state in your report up the chain: "Soon after the war started in the area of Vlasenica municipality (21 April 1992), a special purpose platoon was formed in the Vlasenica SJB in order to realise goals, and on the basis of agreement and suggestions of the Birac SAO government ..." And then you say in the next paragraph: "In order to carry out the order by the Minister of Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina ... 27 July ... this unit has been transformed in such a way that it became part of a reserve contingent, part was transferred into the military police of the main command of Crna Rijeka ..." which means military police of the Main Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "And part was given to the Serbian army. "This unit ... no longer exists ..." So, first of all, August 1992 is when we talked earlier about the mosque being blown up and we confirmed that by that time there was only a handful of Muslims left in Vlasenica. So once the unit that made Muslims disappear without a trace had made all of the Muslims disappear without a trace except for a handful and the supreme commander's forces blew up the mosque, at that point you disbanded this unit; correct?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: If one was to go by dates, that is so. However, as of the moment this platoon was attached to the TO, the Intervention Platoon, that is, of the TO to the police station, we kept asking constantly that the unit be disbanded, removed, or dealt with in another way. Ultimately, none of their members had the conditions to be employed by the Ministry of the Interior and to work in the police because they had not been trained to do so. It was for those reasons that we kept intervening and the sequence of events was such that the minister indeed ordered that the unit be disbanded. We undertook that immediately so that the station could operate in keeping with the Law on Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, in your question did you say that the supreme commander's forces blew up the mosque?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What did you mean by "supreme commander"?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, VRS, blew up the mosque, his forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Exactly, that's my point, sir. As soon as you got the order to disband this unit, it was disbanded; right?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Before that, you said in your statement, you didn't have time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I tender this document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6192, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right, 65 ter 24719 is the last topic, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry this does not have a translation so we'll -- may have to mark it but there's very little that needs to be translated. It just didn't have time -- there is a translation. I thought there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: While it's coming up, just to save time, this is a list of SJB Vlasenica reserve militia -- reserve police force, I should say, sorry, at the Vlasenica SJB security station. If you look at persons listed under number 76 and number 77, it's Miroslav Kraljevic and Elvis Djuric, commander and deputy commander of the special unit; right.

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: They stayed in the MUP; right?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Miroslav Kraljevic was seriously wounded sometime in August. He was then hospitalised in the VMA. For that reason, he couldn't be deployed anywhere and yet he had to exercise some of his rights such as salary to the extent possible. That's why he was kept on the list. As for Elvis Djuric, he was sent alongside the group of policemen who had the conditions in terms of education to attend training, to attend a course to become regular policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender this document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6193.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's clear we will not hear the evidence of the next witness. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue with your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
