utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll start with what is the newest thing in our recollection. A moment ago, on page 99, you were quoted that part of the unit was given to the army. Which part was given to the army and which part was treated in a different way?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: A part of that unit was given to the army. It was such men who had no conditions or interest to apply to attend a policeman course. They were then given to the army and sent to provide security at Crna Rijeka as far as I know. So some of them were completely dealt with by having then gone to the army, whereas others went to attend a policeman course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 95 you were asked about the composition of the station. You have mentioned it before as well as in your statement that the joint police was no longer trusted. Can you tell us briefly what was the reason for that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not quote anything, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not sure, Your Honour. I think it's okay if we just continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm of the same opinion. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly why the joint police was no longer trusted?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: One of the reasons was because in the previous period, let's say in April, part of the Muslim policemen headed by their commander, the official commander, Fadil Turkovic, took full part in the activities surrounding the procurement of weapons and the police force became divided. Consequently, the patrols could no longer function, or rather, one could not create such a shift which could guarantee security during the working hours. One could not set up a multi-ethnic police patrol that would be able to guarantee it. Given the influence of commander Fadil, the police force became divided. Before the 21st of April we still managed to function in keeping with the Law on the Organisation of Internal Affairs of the former B&H.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since in the Muslim part of the municipality they did not establish a police station, who was in charge of police affairs in that rather large part of Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: They had an active reserve force before the 21st of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, sorry, the part that was not under control of the Serb forces, such as Kasaba and Cerska, who policed those areas?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: There were Muslim policemen. Some of them had left the station and joined the reserve police station in Kasaba. In any case, Muslims for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the ethnic make-up of the police in the Muslim-held territory?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: They were all Muslim. They had an ethnically pure force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 89, which is Exhibit P3216, there is reference to five murders. Are you saying that in the four months of war there were five murders?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: I tried to comment that we processed the cases of five murders, although I'm not familiar with the structure of the crimes. Although it was a time of war, the police undertook full treatment, full investigation on site and records as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the document, P3216, page 10 in English and 12 in Serbian. English is enough. Could we just zoom in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here we can see the perpetrators. Could you indicate the ones that you actually prosecuted? And we have a breakdown here according to ethnic membership. For instance, under numbers 12 and 13, who are those men?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Tesic Roksandic, and under 13 we see Zoran Surkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What ethnicity are they?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: They're Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 16, lines 42 and 45 - so page 16 of the English, please - what ethnicity are the people under 42 and 45?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Stanimir Vidovic is a Serb, and 45, Goran Viskovic, also a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 21 - 21, please - would you take a look at 59, 60, and 61, those numbers. Are there any Serbs under 59?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Zoran Bijelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Under 6; right?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about 60 and 61?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Under 61 we see Mirko Vojvodic and 61 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mladen, son of Sretan; right?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are they --

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 24 in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you just take a look at page 64 and 71, what ethnicity are they?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Sasa Masic, Dragan Dimitrovic, they are Serb. And what other number did you say?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Under 71 we see Janko Pajic, also a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There are more but I don't want to waste any more time --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, just to be clear, I'm a little bit late but this doesn't really arise out of the cross because the cross point was - and he's found one - but that only Muslims were prosecuted for weapons, illegal weapons possession, that's what I took him to, not that no Serbs were ever prosecuted. The ones he's shown here, one of the murders was a Serb killing a Serb, others are for theft. He hasn't put it to the witness what these cases are about. So just to be clear, my suggestion was never that no Serbs were prosecuted for anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you said that you would be moving, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct what has been said here, that these Serbs were prosecuted for murders of Serbs and not Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Well, for the most part they were prosecuted. I can't recall all the crimes, but there were cases where in the main we prosecuted for the murders of Serbs, but for others we couldn't really document it. But this -- it depends on the period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 88 you were -- it was suggested to you that you had said that the Serb side, or rather, the SDS armed people together with the JNA and you explained that that was the result of mobilisation. Now, could you tell us what the position of the SD -- of the Serbian Democratic Party was on the issue of response to call-ups?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Well, the Serbian Democratic Party supported the -- Yugoslavia and that means that it also was in favour or supported the respect for all the laws that were in place, which means that the people should respond to mobilisation. Now, it was a legal obligation of every citizen to respond to a mobilisation call-up under the existing laws then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But despite the legal obligations, not all parties took the same position; correct?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Well, that's correct. It was even proved that the SDA had, already for a year, from sometime in mid-1991, instructed people not to send their young soldiers to the army and not to respond to the mobilisation. We have this case where this Mr. Izet Redzic, when the mobilisation was proclaimed, when he came as an official person, he and the then-deputy Kavazbasic, they went to Banja Luka. They collected and took all the -- or withdrew -- took all the Muslim men who had been mobilised into that unit and took them out. So they created a situation, while only the Serbs remained, so that later they could point this out that someone had actually made this army be all Serb, but that's not true. This was actually their strategy to project that kind of impression --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I'll hear from you, although I know what --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Then I'll just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- what the point is --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was just saying that the first question arguably arose from the cross; the second didn't when it went into the broader issue of different ethnicities' views of mobilisation in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it certainly does arise from that and you can see that from the page that I cited.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, you said that a criminal report was submitted because of the blowing up of the mosque. Was the criminal report drafted for an unknown accused or for known perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Well, no, no --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter requests that the witness repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Interpreters couldn't hear your answer, Mr. Djuric. Could you repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the case of the mosque there was a report submitted to the Prosecutor's office, a case that -- a complaint that was submitted against unknown perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know who the perpetrators were?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: No. Well, had we known, we would not do this, we would not submit a report. We would actually submit a classic criminal report, criminal complaint.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you know of any permission granted by any kind of organ or authorities to allow this kind of behaviour or conduct?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: No, I am not aware of any orders that such activities should be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question did not reflect that I asked whether the central organs or me as the commander ever issued an order that would allow such conduct. This did not make it into the transcript when my question was interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Well, generally observing what your positions were, you could never infer such a conclusion and especially or, more specifically, you never dealt with such specifics or such orders. You never issued such orders or supported it. That is my opinion. That's my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you said that the army could also conduct investigations, would they do that if a commander issued an order to that effect or if he knew who had ordered it?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Most probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now briefly take a look at P6190, the last page. Pages 19 or 20. This is not the last page. I'm referring to the part that was admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 21.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the previous page. I believe that 19 and 20 were admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this the page?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the assault group that is mentioned at the bottom of the page, the Planinci or the mount, what kind of forces is this a reference to?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: This was a reference to the column that was moving from Srebrenica and the information we had was that they crossed the Konjevic Polje communication and were headed for Crni Vrh, which is above Zvornik towards Tuzla, and that they were getting closer to the defence lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please can we have page 2, now. Page 22, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you help us and tell us what is the meaning of these words "1.000 Batkovici," and this is an entry for the 15th of July and then below that it says "Miletic"?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: I cannot comment on this. I don't remember. But as -- since they're mentioning Batkovici here, this probably means that perhaps some 1.000 people were moving towards Batkovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see the eight pages further from this spot. I believe the end of the ERN is 90. And before that could we just admit this into evidence, this one page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll add this page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the meaning of these words is "Slapovici," and then the third line where it says the safety deposit box or the safe was not opened, what is this a reference to? What is "Slapovici"? What are we talking about here? And then it goes on: Tendency towards looting about 400 buildings and then vault has not been opened?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: I cannot really remember this, but this was probably up there probably towards Srebrenica someplace. I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For what purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, for the purpose of the 12 kilos of gold that somehow appeared, they were found with the perpetrators, whereas here we see that it says that the vault had not been opened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. What page is this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was discussed in Ademovic, the gold. This is 973, that is -- or, rather, 930 is the ERN number. It ends in 930.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the e-court page number? Say it to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: E-court page 30, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, what date is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It should be 27th or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: After 27th --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, sometime after 27 July. I mean, I'll note that the witness had no idea what this referred to, he says. But again -- I mean, I think we either admit the whole thing or -- which is not a -- I think it's not a huge document or piecemeal like this, but under your -- sorry, I'm a little tired. Under your Chamber's prior ruling you would not admit this page, but I don't really have any problem with any page of this document being admitted. I think it's useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that he confirmed his handwriting, although he didn't remember what it is about, there's no harm in admitting this page. We'll do this. We'll add this to the exhibit, page 30. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were asked and there was a suggestion in that question that you had seen a couple of thousand of people on those buses. Could you tell us how many buses did you see from Vidikovac passing by there at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Well, this column was rather long; however, I couldn't count the buses at that very point -- at that very moment. But later on I learned from some conversations that I had that there were some 50 to 60 buses, mostly buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, how big were these buses and how many people could they take on average?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Well, on average it would be about -- they could bus about 45 people on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. On page 62 it was also mentioned that there were Muslim civilians who had been killed in the village. Now, were these civilians armed or was there shooting on both sides? And this was in Drum.

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't take part in that operation but I heard about it. There was an action underway there and probably there was some kind of provocation which then triggered this shooting, but I cannot claim with certainty whether these civilians were armed or not. But in any case, this did happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, how much longer do you need?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe about five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could conclude as soon as possible. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were asked today, or rather, it was put to you, you were asked whether there was a threat to Zvornik from these forces that were in that area. Was this threat only a threat against Zvornik and how long did this threat to Zvornik from Muslim forces that were around in the woods, how long did it go on for?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Well, in the area above Zvornik, towards Udrc, we had information that there were about some 3.000 to 4.000 men in the column. Later on we established that over 80 per cent of them were, in fact, soldiers who had -- who -- who had changed clothes. But this original -- this initial information that there was some 3.000 to 4.000 men, that wasn't correct. There were far many more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But can you tell us whether this threat to Zvornik was long-lasting? How long did it go on for?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a threat to Zvornik until the moment when the commander, Colonel Pandurevic, ordered that an opening be made towards Tuzla. But then there was still a threat because of all these groups that were around there in that area and it was a threat to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see 1D1220. This document has been translated. It is actually 1D21220. The date is the 1st of August and it was sent to your station from Milici. 1D21220. That's not it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While waiting for it, can you tell us when was this law adopted, when the state security was taken out of MUP and when the names were changed?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: I can't recall exactly. I think it was in 1992, as of, say, April on. I can't be precise. I do know that they separated the public security and the state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 1st of August, 1995, Tomislav Savkic asked -- well, you can see it there. He says several thousand soldiers made a break through along that axis and there are another 1500 left. He also says that Milici is under threat. It was already the 1st of August. What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: As I've said already, the column which went through left behind sizeable groups which moved about the territory of Birac region between Srebrenica and Tuzla. There was a danger for the inhabitants and settlements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It doesn't really arise much from the cross, but no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That's why I asked you. We'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3103, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It does arise. It was mentioned that there was a threat to Zvornik. In any case, the last question, since I don't want to take up anyone else's time anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djuric, have you ever seen a written report or any kind of written communication reporting on the killing of Srebrenica prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: No, I have never seen that report directly. I only received some information later on through these statements, testimonies, and whatnot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After July 1995 have you ever had occasion to meet, the two of us?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djuric. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't -- haven't asked to do this ever before, but there was a question put to the witness about what the "1.000 Batkovic" meant in his handwritten notebook, and he said he couldn't remember exactly what it meant. He discussed this in his interview with me in June 2010, gave a little bit more. I don't know if -- I think it might be useful to refresh his recollection on what he said then and just see if it helps him remember or not, but I realise that it's -- my part is done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have that up again, it's 24 -- P6190, page 20 in both languages -- sorry, sorry, 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This will come up in a minute, sir. Here is what you said when we asked you about this in your interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is at page 48 for my friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [As read] "A thousand Batkovic, Bratunac, I don't know what it was. Some information, it is mentioned here Miletic where it was the fact that I mentioned earlier that I was convinced they are going to Bratunac, something like that. "Q. What's the word after 'Bratunac'? 'No'? "Batkovic. No. I either asked, somebody told me, or I passed this information. I was still convinced that they were going to Batkovic. "Q. Yeah, but then you wrote 'no' because you found out they weren't?" You: "Most probably somebody said no, that they are not. "You don't remember who told you? "No, no, it says here 'Miletic' but it's referred to as Miletic. I don't think I communicated with him." So does that at all help you remember, would be my question?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: It is all in the area of simply noting down events. It is difficult to establish a link from this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Djuric. Thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go. Mr. Robinson, I wanted to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- make an observation with respect to your comment about usage of bar table motion. I will do that first thing on Monday morning. The hearing is adjourned -- I'm sorry, I didn't see you. You were hiding. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll keep that in mind, Mr. President, by way of this location. Just by way of the reference I made earlier to Court's earlier decisions about statements, I think the Court can turn to September 27, 2011, the transcript pages 11819 -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that was 19496 and lines 13 through 24, I believe, and I think that was 27 September 2011. It was one I was able to find quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I thank the staff, interpreters and reporters, for their indulgence. Hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 11th day of March, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.04 p.m.,
